sections.title: The one expression you cannot fake
sections.narration: You can fake a smile. You can arrange your face into a frown, a look of surprise, even a convincing yawn. But try to make yourself blush on purpose and you will fail. Charles Darwin noticed this long before modern psychology existed. In his 1872 book The Expression of the Emotions in Man and Animals, he gives blushing its own chapter, and he opens with a bold statement: "Blushing is the most peculiar and the most human of all expressions." He adds that monkeys redden from passion, but that it would take overwhelming evidence to make him believe any animal could blush. That is a claim we should treat with care, since Darwin could only rely on observers who wrote to him, and we cannot check every animal he never saw. Still, the question he raises is a good one. Why does a thing that nobody wants, that nobody can summon, and that often feels embarrassing, exist at all? Let us look at what Darwin noticed, and where we should stay cautious.

sections.title: The harder you fight it, the worse it gets
sections.narration: Darwin makes a point that anyone who has ever blushed in a meeting will recognize. He says that you cannot cause a blush by touching the body. Tickling makes you laugh and a blow makes you cry out, but a blush needs the mind to be affected. And then comes his sharpest observation: "Blushing is not only involuntary; but the wish to restrain it, by leading to self-attention actually increases the tendency." In other words, the effort to stop a blush makes you think about your face, and thinking about your face makes you blush. It is a small trap built into the mind. Darwin makes self-attention the fundamental element of the whole experience. Today we might say that blushing is tied to being aware of how others see us. Modern researchers still study embarrassment and social self-awareness, though they debate its exact causes, and nobody would claim Darwin had the last word. But his central observation, that watching yourself feeds the blush, remains a surprisingly useful thing to know.

sections.title: Why babies do not blush
sections.narration: One of the cleverest parts of Darwin's chapter is about age. He notes that "The young blush much more freely than the old, but not during infancy". Infants redden with anger from a very early age, but he found no reliable accounts of a blush in the very youngest. He collected reports of two little girls blushing between the ages of two and three, and of another sensitive child, a year older, blushing when reproved for a fault. From this he argued that the mental powers of infants are not yet developed enough to allow it. Notice what this implies. If a blush needs a mind that can imagine being judged, then it is not just a reflex of the blood vessels. It depends on thought. Darwin's evidence here is a handful of anecdotes sent by acquaintances, which a modern scientist would call thin. Even so, the idea that blushing grows with our understanding of other people's eyes fits with how children's social awareness develops, and it is a fair place to begin.

sections.title: A family that could not stop
sections.narration: Darwin also asks whether the tendency to blush runs in families. He reports the case of a household of a father, a mother and ten children, "all of whom, without exception, were prone to blush to a most painful degree". Some of the grown children were sent traveling in the hope of wearing the tendency away, and, he says, nothing helped. He adds a delightful story of the surgeon Sir James Paget, who noticed a girl blushing in an unusual pattern, with big splashes of red appearing first on one cheek and then scattered over the face and neck. When Paget asked the mother whether her daughter always blushed that way, the mother answered yes, she takes after me, and then blushed in exactly the same pattern herself. It is a charming anecdote, but it is only an anecdote. A single family cannot prove inheritance, because families share habits and surroundings as well as genes. Darwin was collecting clues, not running a controlled study, and he would likely be the first to say so.

sections.title: One blush calls another
sections.narration: Darwin describes the physical side with great care. The face, ears and neck are usually the parts that redden, though many people feel their whole body grow hot and tingle. The reddening is followed, he says, by a slight pallor, because the tiny blood vessels first widen and then contract. And he makes a lovely everyday remark: "Every one must have noticed how easily after one blush fresh blushes chase each other over the face." Anyone who has tried to calm themselves after blushing knows the feeling: you notice the heat, you worry that others have noticed it, and the worry sends another wave. He explains the mechanism as a loosening of the small muscles that control the vessels, which lets blood flow in, and he points out that this is not caused by the heart itself. Some of his physiology was based on the knowledge of his day, and later science has refined it considerably. But the picture of a loop, where noticing feeds more of the same, matches his larger point about self-attention.

sections.title: The woman who felt red but looked pale
sections.narration: Here is a story that shows how strange the whole thing is. Darwin reports a young lady at a crowded party who caught her hair so firmly on the button of a passing servant that it took some time to free her. In his account, "from her sensations she imagined that she had blushed crimson; but was assured by a friend that she had turned extremely pale". Think about that. She felt sure that her face was red. In truth, it was the opposite. What she felt was her own sense of being exposed, not the color on her face. This is a quiet warning for all of us. When we are embarrassed, we tend to assume that everyone can see it clearly, and often they cannot. Researchers today call something like this the spotlight effect, the habit of overestimating how much others notice us. Darwin never used that name, and it would be a stretch to credit him with it, but his anecdote points in the same direction.

sections.title: Learning that someone is watching
sections.narration: Darwin ends with a most thoughtful case. Even people born blind blush. He reports that three of the seven or eight blind children at one asylum were great blushers, and that the head of the Worcester College told him: "it is a most important part of their education, as Mr. Blair informs me, to impress this knowledge on their minds", meaning the knowledge that they are being observed. The blind are not at first aware of being watched, so their teachers must teach it, and once they learn it the habit of self-attention grows and the blushing grows with it. This supports Darwin's main idea in a neat way: you do not need to see a face to feel judged, you need only to understand that you can be seen. For us the lesson is gentle. A blush is not weakness or a failing. It is the body showing that you care how you appear to others, which is part of living among people.
